subject: biology
title: Core practicals: cells and physiology
key_idea: These core practicals use living material to test biological ideas: caffeine and Daphnia heart rate, alcohol or temperature and membrane permeability, root tip squashes to see mitosis, respiration rate, spirometer traces and habituation. Each needs a control, careful variables and ethical handling of living things.

blocks.text: Daphnia are small water fleas with a transparent body, so the heart can be seen under a microscope. The effect of caffeine, a stimulant, on heart rate can be measured.

items.text: Make caffeine solutions of different concentrations by dilution, plus a control in pond water only.
Put a Daphnia in a small amount of solution on a cavity slide, with cotton wool fibres to hold it still.
Leave it for a fixed time, for example 5 minutes, so the solution takes effect.
Count heartbeats for a fixed time, such as 30 seconds, under a low-power microscope, and calculate beats per minute.
Use a fresh Daphnia for each concentration, and rinse and rest between tests.

items: Control temperature, time in solution, size and age of Daphnia, and volume of solution.
Caffeine raises the heart rate in Daphnia. Higher concentrations may be harmful.
Daphnia are living animals. Use as few as possible, handle with care, return them to pond water afterwards, and keep them under the light for as short a time as you can.
Counting heartbeats is difficult, so repeats and a stopwatch help.
Count beats per minute with a control for comparison.
Handle Daphnia gently and use the fewest possible.

sections.heading: Membrane permeability and a root tip squash

blocks.text: Two core practicals use plant tissue. One tests how a membrane responds to alcohol or heat, the other shows chromosomes in dividing cells.
Effect of alcohol or temperature on membrane permeability

items: Beetroot cells hold a red pigment (betalain) in their vacuoles, kept in by the membranes.
Cut equal-sized pieces of beetroot, rinse them, and place one in each tube of a range of alcohol concentrations or at a range of temperatures, in a water bath.
Leave for the same time. Remove the beetroot.
Higher alcohol concentrations and higher temperatures damage the membranes (they dissolve phospholipids and denature proteins), so more pigment leaks out.
Measure the pigment with a colorimeter, using a blue-green filter. The higher the absorbance, the greater the permeability.
Control the size and surface area of the beetroot pieces, the volume of liquid and the time.
Mitosis happens in the meristem near the tip of a root, so cells there are dividing.
Hydrochloric acid breaks down the middle lamella, which separates the cells.
A stain such as toluidine blue or acetic orcein colours the chromosomes.
Squashing spreads the cells into a single layer thin enough for light to pass through.

diagram.alt: Put the steps of a root tip squash in order.
diagram.prompt: Put these steps of making a root tip squash in order.
steps: Cut a few millimetres from the tip of a root
Warm the tip in hydrochloric acid
Place it on a slide and add stain
Add a coverslip and squash gently

items: The stages seen are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, plus interphase.
Count the cells in each stage in a field of view, and many fields.
The stage with the most cells is the one that lasts longest.
The **mitotic index** is the number of cells in mitosis ÷ the total number of cells.
More pigment out of beetroot means more damaged membranes.
Acid and stain make a root tip squash show chromosomes.

blocks.text: Two core practicals investigate the rate of respiration and the effect of exercise on breathing.

items: A respirometer measures the oxygen taken up by living organisms, such as germinating seeds, insects or yeast.
Carbon dioxide produced is absorbed by soda lime or potassium hydroxide, so any change in gas volume is the oxygen used.
The liquid in a capillary tube moves towards the organisms as oxygen is used. The distance it moves in a set time gives the rate.
Use a control tube with glass beads in place of the organisms, and keep it in a water bath to hold the temperature steady.
Compare rates at different temperatures or with different organisms.
Allow time for the temperature to settle before starting.
A spirometer records the volume of air breathed in and out. The trace rises and falls as the person breathes.
**Tidal volume** is the volume of air in each normal breath.
**Breathing rate** is the number of breaths per minute.
**Minute ventilation** is the total volume of air breathed in one minute.
**Oxygen consumption** is found from the fall in the trace over time, as the carbon dioxide is absorbed. The gradient of the trace gives the rate.
Exercise increases tidal volume, breathing rate, minute ventilation and oxygen consumption, because muscles respire faster.

blocks.label: Minute ventilation
blocks.formula: minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate
where: minute ventilation = in dm³ per minute
breathing rate = in breaths per minute

diagram.alt: A minute ventilation calculation with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: A student has a tidal volume of {tv} dm³ and a breathing rate of {br} breaths per minute. Calculate the minute ventilation in dm³ per minute.
working: Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.

items: A respirometer follows oxygen uptake once the carbon dioxide is absorbed.
Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.

blocks.text: Habituation is a learned decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is neither helpful nor harmful. It is investigated in animals such as woodlice, snails or earthworms, or in simple human responses.

items: Apply a stimulus, such as a gentle touch, a puff of air or a shadow, and record the response, for example whether a snail withdraws.
Repeat the stimulus at regular intervals and count how many times it takes before the response stops.
Compare with a different or stronger stimulus: the response returns, which shows the animal is not just tired.
Control the strength of the stimulus, the time between stimuli, the temperature, light and noise.
Use animals humanely: handle them gently, use the fewest, avoid stress and return them to their habitat.
Habituation stops an animal wasting energy on unimportant stimuli.
It lets the animal respond to new, more important stimuli, such as a predator.
Habituation is a reduced response to a stimulus that is repeated and harmless.
A new stimulus restores the response, showing it is not fatigue.

checks.q: Explain why a control group with no caffeine is needed when investigating the effect of caffeine on Daphnia heart rate.
checks.a: To show the heart rate under normal conditions; so any change in heart rate can be attributed to caffeine and not to other factors (such as temperature, handling or light).

checks.q: Explain why more red pigment leaks from beetroot placed in a high concentration of ethanol.
checks.a: Ethanol dissolves the phospholipids in the cell membrane (and denatures membrane proteins); so the membranes become more permeable; so the pigment leaks out of the vacuole and the cell.

checks.q: A person has a tidal volume of 0.5 dm³ at rest and a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute. During exercise the breathing rate is 30 breaths per minute and the tidal volume is 2.0 dm³. Calculate the change in minute ventilation.
checks.a: Rest: 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 dm³ per minute; exercise: 2.0 × 30 = 60 dm³ per minute; increase = 53 dm³ per minute.
